title: Curves Defined by Parametric Equations
overview:
A graph $y = f(x)$ can only draw curves that pass the vertical line test: one $y$ for each $x$. A circle fails. So does the path of a thrown ball drawn over time, or any curve that loops or crosses itself. **Parametric equations** fix this by giving both coordinates as functions of a third variable, the **parameter**, usually $t$:
$$x = f(t), \qquad y = g(t).$$
Think of $t$ as time and $(f(t), g(t))$ as the position of a moving point. The curve is the trail the point leaves. The equations carry more information than a plain graph: not just where the point goes, but when, and in which direction.

To sketch a parametric curve, make a table. Pick several $t$ values, compute $x$ and $y$ for each, plot the points, and connect them in order of increasing $t$, adding arrows for direction. The direction matters; the same curve traced backward is a different parametric curve.

Sometimes you can **eliminate the parameter**: solve one equation for $t$ and substitute into the other, producing a relation between $x$ and $y$ alone. That identifies the shape (a parabola, a line, an ellipse), but you must then restore any restrictions the parametrization imposed. For example $x = e^t$, $y = e^{2t}$ gives $y = x^2$, but only the half with $x > 0$ is ever reached.

The most important parametrization is the circle: $x = r\cos t$, $y = r\sin t$ traces the circle of radius $r$ counterclockwise, starting at $(r, 0)$, once for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$. Stretching gives the ellipse $x = a\cos t$, $y = b\sin t$. These work because $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$; eliminating $t$ uses that identity.

A single curve has infinitely many parametrizations. The line segment from $(1, 2)$ to $(4, 8)$ can be walked quickly or slowly, forward or backward. The curve is the same; the motion is not.
keyIdeas: A parametric curve is given by $x = f(t)$, $y = g(t)$ for $t$ in some interval; each $t$ produces one point, and the curve is traced in the direction of increasing $t$.
Parametric curves need not pass the vertical line test; circles, loops, and self-crossings are all allowed.
Eliminating the parameter (solving one equation for $t$ and substituting) reveals the Cartesian shape, but may hide restrictions on which part of that shape is traced.
The circle of radius $r$: $x = r\cos t$, $y = r\sin t$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, counterclockwise from $(r, 0)$. The ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$: $x = a\cos t$, $y = b\sin t$.
Different parametrizations can trace the same set of points at different speeds or in opposite directions; the parametrization is extra information, not just the shape.

workedExamples.title: Table, sketch, eliminate
workedExamples.problem: Sketch the curve $x = t^2$, $y = t + 1$ for $-2 \le t \le 2$, and find its Cartesian equation.
steps: Plot and connect in order of $t$. The point starts at $(4, -1)$, sweeps left to $(0, 1)$, then back right to $(4, 3)$. Arrows point upward throughout since $y = t + 1$ always increases.

Eliminate the parameter: from $y = t + 1$, $t = y - 1$, so $x = (y - 1)^2$. This is a parabola opening to the right with vertex $(0, 1)$, which fails the vertical line test; parametric form handled it with no trouble.
Restriction: $t$ runs from $-2$ to $2$, so $y = t + 1$ runs from $-1$ to $3$. Only the piece of the parabola with $-1 \le y \le 3$ is traced.

workedExamples.title: An ellipse from sine and cosine
workedExamples.problem: Identify the curve $x = 3\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, and describe how it is traced.
steps: Isolate the trig functions: $\cos t = \frac{x}{3}$ and $\sin t = \frac{y}{2}$.
Use $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$: $\frac{x^2}{9} + \frac{y^2}{4} = 1$. An ellipse centered at the origin, reaching $x = \pm 3$ and $y = \pm 2$.
Direction: at $t = 0$ the point is $(3, 0)$; at $t = \frac{\pi}{2}$ it is $(0, 2)$; at $t = \pi$ it is $(-3, 0)$. It moves counterclockwise.

Coverage: as $t$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$ the point goes around exactly once and returns to $(3, 0)$. If the interval were $0 \le t \le 4\pi$ the same ellipse would be traced twice; the set of points is the same, the curve as a motion is different.

workedExamples.title: Parametrizing a line segment
workedExamples.problem: Find parametric equations for the segment from $(1, 2)$ to $(4, 8)$, traced from the first point to the second.
steps: Start at the first point when $t = 0$ and move by the displacement $(4 - 1, 8 - 2) = (3, 6)$ as $t$ goes from $0$ to $1$.
Eliminate $t$: $t = \frac{x - 1}{3}$, so $y = 2 + 2(x - 1) = 2x$. The segment lies on the line $y = 2x$, restricted to $1 \le x \le 4$.
Alternative parametrizations: $x = 4 - 3t$, $y = 8 - 6t$ walks the same segment in reverse; $x = 1 + 3t^2$, $y = 2 + 6t^2$ walks it forward but speeds up. Same points, different motions.

workedExamples.title: A hidden restriction
workedExamples.problem: Describe the curve $x = e^t$, $y = e^{2t}$ for all real $t$.
steps: Eliminate: $y = e^{2t} = \left(e^t\right)^2 = x^2$. So the points lie on the parabola $y = x^2$.
But $x = e^t$ is always positive. As $t \to -\infty$, $x \to 0$ but never reaches it; as $t \to \infty$, $x \to \infty$. Only the right half of the parabola, $x > 0$, is traced.
Direction: $x$ increases with $t$, so the point moves up and to the right, away from the origin.
Lesson: eliminating the parameter gives the shape; reading the ranges of $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ tells you which part of the shape and in which direction. Always do both.

commonMistakes: Plotting $(t, x)$ or $(t, y)$ instead of $(x, y)$. The parameter is not an axis; it labels the points. Check: for $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$ the picture should be a circle, not a wave.

Forgetting direction. After eliminating the parameter, go back and mark arrows using two or three $t$ values. For $x = \cos t$, $y = -\sin t$ the circle is traced clockwise, the opposite of the standard one.
Eliminating the parameter and then claiming the whole Cartesian curve. $x = e^t$, $y = e^{2t}$ gives only the $x > 0$ half of $y = x^2$. Check the range of each coordinate function.

Writing the ellipse as $x = 3\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$ and then reading its equation as $\frac{x^2}{3} + \frac{y^2}{2} = 1$. The denominators are the squares: $9$ and $4$. Test the point $t = 0$, which is $(3, 0)$: $\frac{9}{9} + 0 = 1$.
whyItMatters: Parametric curves are how calculus describes motion: a position depending on time, with velocity and speed to follow in the next section. The arc length formula becomes especially natural here, $\int \sqrt{(dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2}\,dt$, because $dx/dt$ and $dy/dt$ are the velocity components. Polar coordinates are a special parametrization with $\theta$ as the parameter, and vector functions in multivariable calculus are parametric curves in three dimensions. Every curve you integrate along later will be given this way.

checkYourself.q: Where is the point $x = 2\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$ when $t = \pi$?
Eliminate the parameter from $x = t - 1$, $y = t^2$.
checkYourself.a: $t = x + 1$, so $y = (x + 1)^2$, a parabola with vertex $(-1, 0)$, all of it traced.

checkYourself.q: Give parametric equations for the segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(5, -3)$.
What part of the line $y = x$ does $x = t^2$, $y = t^2$ trace?
checkYourself.a: Only the ray with $x \ge 0$, traced out and back as $t$ runs through negative and then positive values.

readingGuide: Find the definition of parametric equations and the idea of the parameter as time. Write in your own words what extra information a parametrization carries beyond the shape.
Before reading the solution of the first sketching example, make your own table of $t$ values and plot the points with direction arrows.
Locate the circle parametrization and work out, for yourself, what changes if $t$ is replaced by $2t$ or by $-t$.
Look for the cycloid and follow how its equations come from the motion of a point on a rolling wheel; you do not need to memorize them, only to see how geometry produced them.
Find any example where eliminating the parameter loses part of the curve, and note how the author restores the restriction.
